rationale: Scanner and protocol differences between sites probably shift the connectivity features more than ADHD does. Because the model is trained on all sites pooled but scored within each site, the classifier may be spending its capacity on site differences. This change standardizes each connectivity edge within each site (using training-fold statistics, which never touch labels), so the linear model only learns from variation inside a site.

ADHD-200's 8 sites differ a lot in scanner, TR and protocol. That likely adds big site-specific offsets to the connectivity features, which the single global classifier can mistake for diagnostic signal, while the score only rewards ranking within each site. I'll standardize every connectivity edge per site, using that site's training-fold mean and SD, before fitting the same L2 logistic regression. This is label-free harmonization in the style of ComBat's location/scale step.

I'm replacing Pearson correlation with Ledoit-Wolf shrunk covariances projected into the Riemannian tangent space. Many ADHD-200 scans have fewer timepoints (about 120–260) than CC200 has ROIs, so Pearson matrices are noisy and rank-deficient. Shrinkage plus a tangent-space embedding is the most reliable connectivity representation in large rs-fMRI benchmarks (Dadi et al. 2019). The reference mean is computed only from the time series, never from labels.

I'm replacing the Fisher-z Pearson edges with a tangent-space embedding of Ledoit-Wolf shrunk covariance matrices, using the same CC200 atlas and the same L2 logistic regression. Benchmarks (Dadi et al. 2019) found this the strongest connectivity measure for rs-fMRI classification. The shrinkage keeps covariances stable when scans have fewer timepoints than ROIs or some ROIs are all zero, and the reference point is the group's Riemannian mean, computed without labels.

I'm replacing the raw Pearson correlation features with a tangent-space embedding of Ledoit-Wolf shrunk correlation matrices. The reference (Riemannian mean) point is fitted only on the training fold. In large rs-fMRI benchmarks (Dadi et al. 2019), tangent-space features beat Pearson features for diagnosis. They map each subject's connectome relative to the group mean, and the shrinkage keeps the matrices well-conditioned for short scans and for all-zero ROIs outside the field of view.

It also respects the positive-definite geometry of the matrices, which helps the classifier separate subjects. Because scoring is within site, removing each site's mean and scale from every feature (computed without labels, separately on train and test) should let the L2 logistic regression spend its limited capacity on within-site diagnostic signal instead of on site differences.

ADHD-200 sites differ a lot in scanner, protocol and TR, so the connectivity distributions shift by site. A single global logistic regression wastes capacity learning those offsets, which can't help when AUROC is scored within each site. This round z-scores each connectivity edge within each site, using that site's train and test items together (no labels involved), so the classifier only learns ADHD-related variation inside a site.

ADHD-200 sites differ a lot in scanner, protocol, TR and scan length, so site effects inflate the variance of the connectivity features. That makes it harder for the regularized linear model to find the small, consistent ADHD signal, especially since the score only compares subjects within each site. This change z-scores every Fisher-z edge separately within each site, using only features and never labels (train and test subjects of a site together, or the training site's own statistics if the site is missing from the test fold). This simple ComBat-style location/scale harmonization should strip out between-site offsets and leave the variation inside each site.

I'm replacing the Pearson-correlation features with a tangent-space embedding of Ledoit-Wolf shrunk correlation matrices (CC200). The covariance reference point is fit only on the training fold. Benchmarks (Dadi et al. 2019) found tangent space was the most reliable connectivity measure for rs-fMRI phenotype prediction. It respects the SPD geometry of connectivity matrices and removes shared group structure, which should make subject-level ADHD differences easier to separate, especially for short, noisy scans.
